introduction-the-poisoned-well-problem.core: Most of what you ship comes from dependencies, base images and build tools. Securing the supply chain means knowing what's inside (SBOM), finding known flaws (scanning), proving who built it (signing) and how (provenance).

first_principles.problem: Attackers target the build and dependency pipeline (SolarWinds, Codecov, xz) because one compromise reaches thousands.
truths: Your code is a small fraction of the artifact.
Artifacts can be tampered with between build and deploy.

analogy.title: Building with Lego from unknown suppliers
analogy.story: You glue together bricks made elsewhere, so you need to check each brick's origin and integrity.
analogy.breaks: Each control covers one gap. You need all of them together.

example.title: The Codecov breach
flow: Thousands of CI runs exfiltrate secrets

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Verify the integrity of everything you pull into CI.

check.q: What are the four core supply-chain controls?
check.a: SBOM generation, vulnerability scanning, signing and build provenance (SLSA).

sboms-the-ingredients-label.core: An SBOM lists every package in an artifact (name, version, licence, hashes) in SPDX or CycloneDX format. Tools like Syft generate it from images or source at build time.

first_principles.problem: When a CVE drops, you can't tell which of hundreds of images contain the vulnerable library.
truths: Images contain OS and language packages.

analogy.title: A food ingredients label
analogy.story: You check for peanuts before eating, and SBOMs let you check for log4j before deploying.
analogy.breaks: SBOMs miss things that weren't installed through package managers (copied binaries).

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: The SBOM travels with the image, signed.

code.text:
syft ghcr.io/acme/api:1.4 -o cyclonedx-json > sbom.json
cosign attest --predicate sbom.json --type cyclonedx ghcr.io/acme/api:1.4

check.q: Name the two main SBOM formats.

vulnerability-scanning-with-grype.core: Grype matches SBOM or image contents against vulnerability databases and reports CVEs by severity. In CI it can fail builds above a threshold, and re-scanning stored SBOMs catches newly disclosed CVEs.

first_principles.problem: An ingredients list is useless unless you know which ingredients are dangerous today.
truths: Severity and fix availability guide priority.
Gates must be tuned to avoid alert fatigue.
derivation: Use **--fail-on high** as a CI gate.
Use **--only-fixed** to focus on actionable items.

analogy.title: A recall checker
analogy.story: It compares your pantry list against today's recall notices.
analogy.breaks: Scanners report presence, not exploitability, so triage with reachability or VEX.

example.title: A CI gate
example.scenario: Fail on high with a fix available.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Builds with fixable high CVEs are blocked.

check.q: Why re-scan SBOMs of already-deployed images?
check.a: New CVEs are disclosed after deployment, so yesterday's clean image can be vulnerable today.

image-signing-the-digital-wax-seal.core: Signing an image digest cryptographically binds it to the signer. Verifying the signature at deploy proves the image is exactly what the trusted pipeline produced and hasn't been tampered with since.

first_principles.problem: An attacker who can push to the registry, or intercept traffic, can replace a scanned, clean image with malware.
truths: Verification must happen at the point of use.

analogy.title: A wax seal on a letter
analogy.story: A broken or missing seal shows the letter was opened or forged.
analogy.breaks: A signature proves origin, not safety. A trusted pipeline can still sign vulnerable code.

steps.label: Policy
steps.detail: The cluster refuses unsigned or tampered images.

code.text:
cosign sign ghcr.io/acme/api@sha256:ab12...
cosign verify ghcr.io/acme/api@sha256:ab12... --certificate-identity ... --certificate-oidc-issuer ...

check.q: Why sign the digest rather than the tag?
check.a: Tags can be moved to point at different content, while a digest uniquely identifies exact bytes.

sigstore-and-keyless-signing-a-revolutio.core: Sigstore removes long-lived signing keys. Fulcio issues a short-lived certificate bound to an OIDC identity (for example a GitHub Actions workflow), and Rekor records the signature in a public transparency log, so you trust identities, not key files.

first_principles.problem: Managing, rotating and protecting private signing keys is hard, and leaked keys are catastrophic.
truths: OIDC identities already exist in CI.
derivation: **Fulcio** issues a 10-minute cert for that identity.
Sign; record in the **Rekor** transparency log.
Verify by **identity + issuer**, not by key.

analogy.title: Signing a register with your ID at the front desk
analogy.story: Instead of carrying a personal stamp that could be stolen, you show ID and sign a public ledger.
analogy.breaks: Verification policies must pin the expected identity, or any GitHub workflow could sign.

check.a: An append-only public transparency log of signatures, making misuse detectable.

provenance-and-slsa-the-roadmap-to-trust.core: Provenance is a signed record of how an artifact was built: source repo and commit, builder, parameters. SLSA levels define how trustworthy it is, from 'it exists' up to 'generated by a hardened, isolated builder that the build can't tamper with'.

first_principles.problem: Knowing what's inside and who signed it doesn't prove the build wasn't manipulated.
truths: Provenance generated by the platform is harder to forge.
derivation: Have it generated by the **build platform**, not by user scripts.

analogy.title: A recipe card stamped by a certified kitchen
analogy.story: It's not just the ingredient list, but where and how the dish was made, certified by the kitchen itself.
analogy.breaks: SLSA doesn't guarantee the source code is free of malicious commits.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: You confirm it came from that repo and tag via the trusted builder.

code.text:
slsa-verifier verify-artifact app.tar.gz \
  --provenance-path app.intoto.jsonl \
  --source-uri github.com/acme/app --source-tag v1.4.0

check.q: What does SLSA provenance add beyond an SBOM and a signature?
check.a: A verifiable record of how and where the artifact was built (source, builder, process).
